implementation_notes: The direct realization: assert raises AssertionError when the condition is false in normal mode, __post_init__ is a useful check site for dataclasses, and properties or __setattr__ can guard mutations. The whole statement is removed by the compiler under -O or PYTHONOPTIMIZE, which makes this the right carrier for development-time invariants and the wrong one for a rule that must hold in production. Validate caller input with explicit exceptions; use pytest and Hypothesis to reuse the predicate as a test oracle.
pitfalls: python -O removes every assert statement, so production-critical invariants written this way silently disappear; use an explicit raise for those.
Because assertions can vanish, predicates must be side-effect free - an assertion that calls a mutating method behaves differently under -O.
AssertionError is not a validation error: raising it on user input makes a bad request indistinguishable from a programming bug.

variants.name: Always-on guarded raise in constructors and mutators
variants.idiom_name: raise ValueError/InvariantError with a named check method
variants.implementation_notes: When the invariant must hold in optimized builds too, replace assert with an explicit raise: a private check_invariants() method invoked from __init__ or __post_init__ and after every mutation, raising a dedicated exception type. This variant is the production-strength sibling of the assert idiom; its cost is that the check runs even when -O strips assertions, and that the exception is an ordinary, catchable one.
pitfalls: A dedicated exception class is essential: raising bare Exception makes the invariant violation indistinguishable from unrelated failures in logs.
Callers can catch the exception, so the fail-fast property must be protected by convention or code review rather than by the language.
Every mutator must call the check; there is no compiler enforcement, and a forgotten call site is exactly the silent-corruption case the pattern exists to prevent.
